title: FinanceLab — Master Open Question Bank (50 Questions)
subtitle: All Chapters · Cross-Chapter Synthesis · PE/IB/M&A Focus
instructions: 50 open-ended questions requiring thorough analytical thinking. Each question integrates concepts from multiple chapters. Graded by Claude API using the provided rubric. These questions reflect the depth expected in IB/PE interviews and M&A due diligence.

questions.question: Explain why a rapidly growing, profitable company can simultaneously be cash-flow negative. Use the three financial statements to tell the complete story, and explain what an investor should think about this situation.
questions.model_answer: A company can be profitable (positive NI on the IS) but cash-flow negative because of accrual timing mismatches. During rapid growth: (1) Revenue is recognized when delivered, but cash collection lags — AR builds on the BS. (2) Inventory is purchased and built ahead of sales — cash leaves but COGS hits the IS only when delivered. (3) Fixed assets (CapEx) are purchased — full cash out in CFI, but only depreciation hits the IS in that period. On the SCF: CFO = NI − ΔAR − ΔInventory + ΔAP + D&A. In fast growth, AR and inventory grow faster than AP, so the working capital drag exceeds NI. CFI is also strongly negative due to CapEx. Result: the company shows profit but burns cash. Investor interpretation: this is normal for healthy growth companies (Amazon 2000–2005). The question is whether working capital efficiency improves as growth slows and the business matures into a cash cow. Red flag if: AR grows faster than revenue (collection problem), inventory grows faster than COGS (demand problem), or CapEx never converts into revenue growth.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) identifying the three accrual sources of the profit-cash gap (AR, inventory, CapEx), (2) explaining the SCF indirect method linkage, (3) giving a balanced investor interpretation (normal in growth vs. warning signs if quality deteriorates), (4) referencing all three statements in the explanation.

questions.question: A PE fund is comparing two consumer goods companies: Company A has ROE of 25%, ROA of 18%, and low debt. Company B has ROE of 25%, ROA of 8%, and high debt. Which is the better business, and how do you use DuPont to support your answer?
questions.model_answer: DuPont: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier (Assets/Equity). Both have ROE = 25%. Company A: ROE = 25% with ROA = 18% → Equity Multiplier = 25/18 ≈ 1.4x → low leverage. Company B: ROE = 25% with ROA = 8% → Equity Multiplier = 25/8 ≈ 3.1x → high leverage. Company A is clearly the better business: its 25% ROE is driven by genuine operating performance (high ROA). Its low leverage means minimal financial risk and strong balance sheet resilience. Company B's identical ROE is an artifact of leverage — borrow enough, and a mediocre business can show the same ROE as an excellent one. If economic conditions deteriorate and ROA falls to, say, 5%, Company A's ROE merely declines gracefully; Company B's ROE collapses and may go negative (ROA < cost of debt → equity destroyed). For PE: a highly leveraged company is a financing story, not a business quality story. In an LBO context, you would add leverage to Company A's excellent fundamentals — not use leverage to mask Company B's mediocrity.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct DuPont decomposition and equity multiplier calculation for both, (2) identifying Company A as the better business, (3) explaining that Company B's ROE is leverage-driven not operationally earned, (4) the risk asymmetry in a downturn, (5) connecting to PE/deal context.

questions.question: You are building an LBO model for a distribution company. The CFO tells you that working capital 'takes care of itself.' Walk through the three components of the Cash Conversion Cycle, explain why working capital absolutely does NOT take care of itself in an LBO, and identify three specific improvements the PE fund could drive post-acquisition.
questions.model_answer: CCC = Inventory Days + DSO − DPO. (1) Inventory Days: cash tied up from purchase to sale. In an LBO, if target carries 90-day inventory, $1bn revenue at 40% COGS = $400m COGS → inventory = $400m × 90/365 = $99m tied up. (2) DSO: cash tied up from sale to collection. At 60-day DSO on $1bn revenue → AR = $164m. (3) DPO: free supplier credit offsetting the above. At 30-day DPO on $400m COGS → AP = $33m. NWC = $99m + $164m − $33m = $230m. In an LBO, NWC matters because: (a) each incremental revenue dollar requires incremental NWC investment, consuming cash that could repay debt; (b) the acquisition NWC is part of the equity check (higher NWC target = higher purchase price); (c) NWC fluctuations affect covenant compliance (liquidity). Three PE improvements: (1) Inventory reduction: SKU rationalization, demand forecasting improvement, JIT-style procurement → cut inventory days from 90 to 60 = $33m cash release. (2) AR improvement: better credit terms, invoicing efficiency, early payment discounts → cut DSO from 60 to 45 = $41m cash release. (3) AP extension: renegotiate supplier payment terms from 30 to 45 days = $16m cash benefit. Total potential one-time cash release: ~$90m — directly available for debt repayment.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct CCC formula and explanation of each component, (2) why NWC matters in an LBO (debt repayment, equity check, covenants), (3) at least three specific, quantified improvement levers, (4) linking NWC improvement to FCF and debt paydown.

questions.question: Walk through the complete accounting impact of an acquisition on the acquirer's financial statements. Cover the Balance Sheet, Income Statement, and Statement of Cash Flows in the acquisition year and in subsequent years.
questions.model_answer: Acquisition year — Balance Sheet: Cash decreases by purchase price. Acquired assets step up to fair value (PPA). Previously off-balance-sheet intangibles (brand, customer relationships, technology) are recognized. Liabilities assumed at fair value. Goodwill = purchase price − revalued net assets appears. If debt-financed: Long-Term Debt increases. Minority Interest appears if <100% acquired. Acquisition year — SCF: CFI shows large outflow (acquisition price paid). If debt financed: CFF shows inflow from new debt. No P&L impact from the acquisition itself — it's a balance sheet transaction. Acquisition year — Income Statement: Consolidated revenue and costs from subsidiary from date of acquisition. Additional amortization of identified intangibles begins. Additional interest expense from acquisition debt. Target's results fully consolidated. Subsequent years — IS: Annual amortization of PPA intangibles (customer lists, technology, brand) → higher D&A charge each year until fully amortized. Higher interest expense from deal debt (declining as debt is repaid). Potential goodwill impairment if business underperforms. Subsequent years — BS: Goodwill remains (no amortization under IFRS) until impaired. PPA intangibles decline as amortized. Debt declines as repaid. Retained earnings grows (net of higher D&A and interest charges). Key insight: EBITDA is unaffected by PPA amortization and interest — which is why it is the pre-deal and post-deal performance metric. Net income is significantly depressed post-LBO.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct BS impact (PPA, goodwill, debt, MI), (2) SCF acquisition year (CFI outflow, CFF if debt-financed), (3) ongoing IS impacts (D&A from PPA, interest on debt), (4) explaining why EBITDA is immune and NI is depressed.

questions.question: A company's EBITDA has grown 20% YoY. Identify five specific earnings management techniques across the areas of revenue recognition, inventory costing, and accounts receivable that could make this growth partially or fully artificial. For each, state the signal an analyst would observe.
questions.model_answer: (1) Premature revenue recognition: Revenue recognized before delivery or before return period expires. Signal: AR grows faster than revenue (rising DSO), high Q4 revenue reversals in Q1. (2) Channel stuffing: Goods pushed to distributors at year-end with liberal return rights. Signal: Inventory at distributors piling up, Q1 sales reversal, rising DSO. (3) LIFO liquidation: Inventory allowed to decline, forcing cheap old LIFO layers into COGS. Signal: Inventory levels fall while revenue is flat; gross margin improves with no operational explanation. (4) Underprovisioning AUA: Setting allowance for uncollectible accounts too low relative to actual bad debt experience. Signal: AUA/Gross AR coverage ratio declining; subsequent large write-offs in later years. (5) NRV write-down avoidance: Holding obsolete or declining-value inventory at cost rather than writing down to NRV. Signal: Inventory days rising dramatically; gross margin holds up despite known market price declines in the industry. Cross-cutting analytical defense: CFO/NI ratio (CRR) declining is the most powerful single indicator that accruals are building across multiple dimensions. Request underlying customer-level AR aging, inventory obsolescence analysis, and comparison of accounting estimates to industry peers.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) at least five distinct techniques across the three areas, (2) each technique correctly described mechanically, (3) a specific observable signal for each, (4) mention of CRR as the integrated indicator.

questions.question: A technology company and a steel mill both have EBITDA of $200m. The tech company has CapEx of $10m and NWC investment of $15m. The steel mill has CapEx of $120m and NWC investment of $5m. Walk through the FCF of each business. Explain what this means for PE investment strategy.
questions.model_answer: FCF = EBITDA − Taxes − CapEx − ΔNWC (pre-tax approximation ignoring taxes for simplicity). Tech: FCF ≈ 200 − 10 − 15 = $175m (87.5% FCF conversion). Steel mill: FCF ≈ 200 − 120 − 5 = $75m (37.5% FCF conversion). Same EBITDA, radically different FCF. For PE strategy: (1) The tech company's high FCF conversion means it can service large amounts of debt — ideal LBO candidate. At 5x leverage ($1bn debt) and 6% interest, interest = $60m, leaving $115m FCF for debt repayment. Debt paydown over 5 years is feasible. (2) The steel mill's low FCF conversion (heavy maintenance CapEx is non-discretionary — assets corrode without it) means it can service far less debt. Same leverage levels would be dangerous. Additional considerations: (3) Tech CapEx is likely growth CapEx (discretionary), making FCF even more resilient. Steel CapEx includes heavy maintenance CapEx that cannot be deferred. (4) EBITDA is a poor proxy for cash flow in capital-intensive industries. (5) EV/EBITDA multiples are not directly comparable across industries — a 10x EV/EBITDA for tech implies far more real cash flow than 10x for steel. This is the fundamental critique of using EBITDA universally.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct FCF calculation for each, (2) FCF conversion ratio comparison, (3) explaining the LBO debt capacity implications, (4) maintenance vs. growth CapEx distinction, (5) challenge to EBITDA as universal benchmark.

questions.question: A retail chain plans to expand from 100 to 150 stores over 3 years. The CFO presents the board with growing net income projections but declining CFO. Explain the accounting and economic reasons for this pattern, and describe what metrics you would use to assess whether the expansion is healthy or troubling.
questions.model_answer: During store rollout, the divergence between NI growth and CFO decline occurs for several reasons: (1) Inventory build: each new store requires opening inventory. 50 new stores × average inventory/store = significant cash out before first sale. This hits CFI (CapEx for fit-out) and CFO (inventory build). (2) Revenue recognition timing: NI grows because new stores generate revenue from Day 1. Cash collection may lag if wholesale or franchise revenues are involved. (3) Prepaid expenses: lease deposits, insurance, etc. are prepaid assets reducing CFO but not immediately hitting the IS. (4) CapEx front-loading: store fit-out CapEx hits CFI immediately; only annual depreciation hits the IS. The NI includes projected steady-state store economics; the CFO reflects the actual cash cost of building out. Healthy expansion signals: (a) Existing (mature) stores have strong same-store EBITDA margins. (b) Inventory Days for mature stores are stable or declining. (c) New store payback period is short (1–2 years). (d) Total portfolio CFO is growing even if FCF is negative (investment period). (e) ROIC on new stores (NOPAT / Incremental Invested Capital) exceeds WACC. Troubling signals: (a) Mature store margins declining (suggesting the concept is weakening). (b) Inventory days rising across the portfolio (not just new stores). (c) Customer purchase frequency declining (NI held up by store count growth masking unit economics deterioration).
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) at least three accounting reasons for NI/CFO divergence, (2) mature store EBITDA as the key health indicator, (3) same-store sales concept, (4) ROIC vs. WACC as the capital allocation test, (5) correctly noting CFO decline can be healthy if driven purely by growth investment.

questions.question: A serial acquirer has made 15 acquisitions over 10 years and carries $3bn of goodwill on its balance sheet. It has never recorded an impairment. An analyst asks: 'Is this balance sheet clean or concerning?' How do you answer?
questions.model_answer: The right answer is: it depends, but the starting posture is concern. Arguments that it is concerning: (1) No impairments over 10 years and 15 deals implies either every acquisition has performed at or above expectations — statistically unlikely given that most academic research shows 50–60% of acquisitions fail to create value. (2) Impairment testing is performed by management using their own assumptions (discount rate, growth rate) — these are gameable. Management has strong incentives to avoid impairment (it's an admission of overpayment and destroys reported book value and ROE). (3) The $3bn goodwill is opaque: which deals does it relate to? What are the underlying business unit performance trends? (4) Goodwill as % of total assets is a leverage on valuation assumptions — a 5–10% change in discount rate assumptions can flip a passing impairment test to a failing one. Diligence steps: (1) Decompose goodwill by acquisition — when was each deal done, at what multiple, has the business unit performed vs. acquisition business case? (2) Analyze impairment test assumptions for conservatism (discount rate, terminal growth rate). (3) Compare goodwill/assets to peers — is this level typical for the industry? (4) Examine each acquired business's EBITDA trajectory since acquisition. (5) Look for evidence of write-downs below the goodwill line (in specific assets) that mask underlying performance issues. Zero impairments across 15 deals is a yellow flag — not necessarily manipulation, but worth probing.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) identifying management's incentives to avoid impairment, (2) noting that impairment assumptions are manageable, (3) proposing deal-by-deal performance analysis, (4) statistical argument (not all 15 deals can be perfect), (5) suggesting specific analytical steps.

questions.question: You are conducting QoE due diligence on a B2B software company. Gross AR has grown from $80m to $140m (+75%) over 2 years while revenue grew from $200m to $260m (+30%). AUA has grown from $4m to $5m. What are your concerns, what analyses would you run, and what are the possible legitimate explanations?
questions.model_answer: Immediate concern: DSO has risen from 80×365/200 = 146 days to 140×365/260 = 197 days. A 51-day increase in DSO is alarming for any business. AUA coverage has fallen from 4/80 = 5% to 5/140 = 3.6% — suggesting either improving collections (unlikely given DSO rise) or underprovisioning. Analyses to run: (1) Disaggregate AR by customer: which specific customers account for the increase? Are they large, creditworthy customers who are simply slow payers, or is AR distributed across many at-risk customers? (2) Aging analysis: what % of AR is >90 days overdue? >180 days? This reveals whether the AR pile-up is chronic or recent. (3) Revenue recognition review: is software revenue being recognized upfront (at signing) rather than ratably? A policy shift to front-loaded recognition would inflate both revenue and AR. (4) Post-period collections: how much of the Dec 31 AR balance was actually collected by Feb 28? Cash collection post-period-end is the acid test. (5) AUA adequacy: compare the allowance to historical bad debt rates. If bad debts historically run at 8–10% of AR but AUA is only 3.6%, it is severely underprovided. Legitimate explanations: (1) New customer mix with longer standard payment terms (e.g., expansion into enterprise segment with 120-day net terms). (2) Revenue model shift to longer-duration contracts with invoicing at delivery. (3) Seasonal patterns where Q4 is heavily back-loaded. In each case, demand the underlying support — customer-level AR schedules, contract terms, and subsequent cash collections.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct DSO calculation and interpretation, (2) AUA coverage analysis, (3) post-period cash collection test, (4) aging analysis, (5) revenue recognition examination, (6) at least one legitimate explanation mentioned.

questions.question: You need to build a simplified three-statement model. Starting from EBITDA of $150m, D&A of $30m, interest of $20m, tax rate of 25%, CapEx of $40m, and an NWC increase of $15m, build through to Free Cash Flow. Then explain how each of the three statements is connected in this model.
questions.model_answer: Income Statement: EBITDA $150m → EBIT = 150−30 = $120m → Pre-tax income = 120−20 = $100m → Tax = 100×25% = $25m → Net Income = $75m. Balance Sheet changes: Retained Earnings +$75m (from NI). PPE net declines by $30m depreciation but increases by $40m CapEx → net PPE +$10m. AR/Inventory +$15m (NWC increase). Debt decreases if any repaid (not given here). Cash changes per SCF. SCF — CFO (indirect): NI $75m + D&A $30m − ΔNWC $15m = CFO $90m. CFI: −$40m (CapEx). CFF: −$20m (if interest paid in CFF under IFRS choice, or stays in CFO under US GAAP). Net Change in Cash: +$30m (if interest in CFO: 90−40 = $50m net; if interest in CFF: $90m−$40m−$20m = $30m). Free Cash Flow = CFO − CapEx = $90m − $40m = $50m. Three-statement connections: (1) NI flows from IS to Retained Earnings on BS. (2) D&A on IS links to accumulated depreciation on BS. (3) CapEx in CFI equals increase in gross PPE on BS. (4) ΔNWC in CFO corresponds to changes in AR, inventory, AP on BS. (5) Net change in Cash per SCF = Change in Cash on BS. The accounting equation must hold at every step.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct IS build to NI, (2) correct CFO calculation, (3) correct FCF = CFO − CapEx, (4) explaining at least three specific IS→BS→SCF linkages, (5) noting the accounting equation constraint.

questions.question: A Czech manufacturing company buys raw materials in USD but reports in CZK. The CZK has depreciated 15% against the USD. The company uses FIFO inventory costing. Explain the impact on the Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and working capital for the current year.
questions.model_answer: Under FIFO, the company sells the oldest (cheapest, pre-depreciation) inventory first. In the current year: (1) COGS is understated relative to current replacement cost — the cheap pre-depreciation inventory is being matched against current revenues priced at new (depreciated CZK) cost levels. Gross margin is artificially inflated. (2) Ending inventory is the most recently purchased (expensive, post-depreciation) inventory — the Balance Sheet inventory value is closer to current replacement cost (this is the FIFO BS advantage). (3) Going forward: the company must replenish inventory at the new, higher CZK cost. Cash used to replenish inventory is 15% higher per unit — a real cash pressure not yet fully reflected in COGS. (4) Working capital impact: inventory value on the BS increases (higher replacement cost), tying up more cash. If the company finances inventory purchases with USD-denominated payables, AP also increases in CZK terms → partially offsetting. The key risk: the company's reported gross margins look good today (FIFO low COGS) but will deteriorate sharply next period when the expensive new inventory moves through COGS. A forward-looking analyst normalizes for this: sustainable gross margin = revenue − COGS at current replacement cost, not historical.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) FIFO low COGS in period of rising costs, (2) BS inventory correctly stated at current cost (FIFO advantage), (3) forward-looking cash replenishment cost pressure, (4) working capital implication of higher replacement cost inventory, (5) analytical normalization needed.

questions.question: You are advising a PE fund on two acquisition targets. Target A (software): Revenue $200m, COGS $40m (variable), SG&A $80m (60% fixed), EBITDA $80m. Target B (industrial): Revenue $200m, COGS $160m (variable), SG&A $10m (all fixed), EBITDA $30m. Model a 20% revenue decline scenario. What does this tell you about risk in each deal?
questions.model_answer: Revenue falls to $160m for both. Target A (software, high fixed costs): COGS variable = falls 20% → $32m. Fixed SG&A = 60%×80 = $48m (doesn't fall). Variable SG&A = 40%×80 = $32m → falls to $25.6m. New EBITDA = 160−32−48−25.6 = $54.4m. EBITDA decline = 80→54.4 = −32%. Revenue fell 20%, EBITDA fell 32% → operating leverage multiplier ≈ 1.6x. Target B (industrial, mostly variable COGS): COGS variable = falls 20% → $128m. Fixed SG&A = $10m (unchanged). New EBITDA = 160−128−10 = $22m. EBITDA decline = 30→22 = −27%. Revenue fell 20%, EBITDA fell 27% → leverage multiplier ≈ 1.3x. Somewhat surprisingly, Target B shows slightly less EBITDA % decline — its high variable COGS provides a natural hedge (costs fall with revenue). Target A's high fixed SG&A creates the leverage problem. PE implications: (1) In an LBO, Target A's higher base EBITDA supports more debt. But in a downturn, EBITDA volatility may breach covenants faster than Target B. (2) Target B's low margin business is riskier in absolute terms (EBITDA of $22m post-decline may not cover interest on any meaningful debt load). (3) The operating leverage vs. debt leverage interaction is critical: high operating leverage + high financial leverage = fragile capital structure in downturns. Conservative LBO underwriting stress-tests the combined leverage effect.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct EBITDA calculation under stress for both companies, (2) identifying fixed vs. variable cost structure, (3) leverage multiplier concept, (4) recognizing Target B's variable costs as natural hedge, (5) PE implications for debt sizing and covenant risk.

questions.question: BuyerCo acquires 80% of SubCo for $640m. SubCo's net assets have book value of $500m and fair value of $600m. Using both the Book Value MI and Market Value MI approaches, calculate goodwill and minority interest. Explain which approach IFRS 3 requires and why the choice matters for valuation.
questions.model_answer: Book Value MI approach: MI = 20% × BV(NA) = 20% × $500m = $100m. Gw = (640 + 100) − 600 = $140m. Market Value MI approach: Implied 100% price = $640m / 0.80 = $800m. MI = $800m − $640m = $160m (at market value). Gw = (640 + 160) − 600 = $200m. IFRS 3 allows BOTH approaches — the choice is made on an acquisition-by-acquisition basis. IFRS 3 calls them: (1) 'Partial goodwill' method = book value MI (only the majority's goodwill recognized). (2) 'Full goodwill' method = market value MI (goodwill recognized for the entire entity). Why it matters for valuation: (1) Full goodwill gives a larger goodwill balance — higher future impairment exposure. (2) Full goodwill gives higher NCI balance — higher equity bridge deduction. (3) In a subsequent buyout of the minority, the full goodwill method has already recognized the minority's share of goodwill, reducing the step-up needed. (4) For the equity value bridge: Equity Value = EV − Net Debt − MI. The MI value used should be the market value (NCI at current fair value), not the book value. Using book value MI in the bridge understates the deduction and overstates equity value.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct MI and Gw under both approaches, (2) identifying IFRS 3 permits both, (3) explaining the goodwill difference, (4) equity bridge implication (MI at market value for bridge), (5) impairment exposure difference.

questions.question: An e-commerce company reports 40% YoY revenue growth. Net income grew 25%. CFO declined 5%. DSO increased from 30 to 52 days. AUA/Gross AR fell from 6% to 3%. Inventory days rose from 45 to 70 days. Assess the quality of this revenue growth.
questions.model_answer: This profile raises serious quality of earnings concerns across every dimension: (1) NI grew at 25% vs revenue 40% — margin compression, not expansion. Something is wrong with cost structure or mix. (2) CFO declined 5% while revenue grew 40% — CRR = roughly 0.6× (bad). Massive accrual build. (3) DSO: 30→52 days on $Y revenue = AR is 73% higher-per-dollar-of-revenue. At 40% revenue growth, AR should grow 40% if DSO is flat. It grew much more. Revenue may be: (a) premature (before return window closed), (b) channel stuffed, (c) granted to marginal credit customers to hit growth targets. (4) AUA coverage halved: either collections genuinely improved (inconsistent with DSO rise), or management is underprovisioning — boosting NI by not recognizing expected bad debt expense. A more honest AUA provision at 6% on the higher gross AR base would significantly reduce reported NI. (5) Inventory days rose from 45 to 70 — inventory is accumulating faster than it is being sold. This could mean: (a) weak underlying demand masked by revenue recognition timing, (b) returns of previously 'sold' goods sitting in inventory, (c) overbuying in anticipation of demand that hasn't materialized. Overall verdict: a significant portion of this 40% revenue growth appears to be accounting-driven, not real business growth. CFO/NI ratio, DSO trend, and AUA underprovision are three independent red flags pointing in the same direction.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) interpreting each metric correctly, (2) linking DSO rise to potential revenue quality issue, (3) AUA underprovision as NI inflation, (4) inventory build as potential demand warning, (5) synthesizing across all signals for a coherent overall verdict.

questions.question: You are presenting normalized EBITDA for an acquisition target to your IC. Reported EBITDA = $120m. Identify at least six categories of potential adjustments and explain the analytical framework for deciding whether to include or exclude each.
questions.model_answer: The framework for EBITDA normalization: include items that are truly non-recurring, non-operational, or accounting-driven distortions of sustainable cash earnings. Exclude items that, while irregular in timing, represent genuine ongoing business costs. Categories: (1) Owner/related-party costs: above-market management fees, excess owner compensation, related-party lease at non-market rent → adjust to market rate (typically add back excess). (2) One-time restructuring charges: if truly one-time (plant closure, severance for eliminated positions), add back. If recurring restructuring every 2–3 years, treat as quasi-recurring → do not add back. (3) Litigation settlements: large, specific, documented one-time events → add back. If the business faces recurring litigation (e.g., product liability), treat as ongoing cost. (4) PPA amortization: added back in EBITDA automatically (D&A add-back). (5) M&A transaction fees (target's advisor, legal fees): one-time → add back. (6) Non-recurring revenue or customer losses: if a major contract ended, adjust EBITDA for the lost contribution to show run-rate (downward adjustment). (7) COVID/weather/extraordinary effects: add back specific documented revenue losses or cost spikes attributable to identifiable external events — but scrutinize management's tendency to blame everything on external factors. (8) Stock-based compensation: often added back in PE EBITDA bridge (non-cash), but represents real economic cost of employee compensation → treat carefully. Red line: do not add back items that are recurring in nature simply because they are labeled 'one-time.' Serial restructurers, companies that 'invest' in M&A every year, and businesses with chronic litigation exposure should have these treated as ongoing costs.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) at least six categories, (2) clear inclusion/exclusion framework, (3) nuanced treatment of 'recurring one-times,' (4) the red line on gaming adjustments, (5) at least one downward QoE adjustment (non-recurring revenue).

questions.question: A company has a Current Ratio of 0.7 and a Quick Ratio of 0.65. A junior analyst concludes the company is in liquidity trouble and will default imminently. Critique this conclusion. What additional information do you need before forming a view?
questions.model_answer: The junior analyst's conclusion is too hasty — these ratios alone are insufficient to conclude distress. Critique: (1) Industry context: many retailers and subscription businesses operate with negative working capital by design (they collect cash before delivering goods/services — deferred revenue is a current liability). Supermarkets typically have Current Ratios below 1.0. These are not distressed — they have very fast inventory turns and negative CCC. (2) The similarity of Current and Quick Ratios (0.7 vs 0.65) implies very little inventory in current assets — inventory is not the problem. The business may simply carry minimal inventory. (3) The absolute amount matters: a company with $5bn in undrawn credit facilities and $500m in current liabilities is not in liquidity trouble despite a low current ratio. (4) Cash generation: a company with $200m CFO and $300m current liabilities is fine even at <1.0 current ratio — it generates cash to meet obligations. Ratios miss the SCF entirely. (5) Debt maturity profile: are the current liabilities short-term debt due imminently (problem) or trade payables (normal operating item)? Additional information needed: (1) Industry benchmark current ratios, (2) undrawn credit facilities / liquidity headroom, (3) CFO run-rate, (4) debt maturity schedule, (5) CCC (negative CCC = deliberate low working capital), (6) seasonal patterns (Q4 current ratio may be artificially low for retail).
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) identifying that <1.0 current ratio is normal for many industries, (2) credit facility / liquidity headroom, (3) CFO as the real liquidity measure, (4) debt maturity composition of current liabilities, (5) CCC context, (6) seasonal effects.

questions.question: You are acquiring a US company with a $150m LIFO reserve. The acquisition will be reported under IFRS (European PE fund). Walk through (a) the accounting conversion at acquisition, (b) the impact on the deal's enterprise value and equity check, and (c) the P&L impact in Years 1–2 post-acquisition.
questions.model_answer: (a) LIFO to IFRS conversion at acquisition: Under IFRS (IAS 2), LIFO is prohibited. PPA must recognize inventory at fair value — effectively FIFO-equivalent. Inventory increases by $150m LIFO reserve. Deferred Tax Liability created: $150m × 25% = $37.5m (the company will owe this tax when the higher-cost inventory is sold). Net equity impact = +$112.5m. The consolidated Opening Balance Sheet shows: Inventory +$150m, DTL +$37.5m, Equity +$112.5m. (b) Enterprise Value and equity check: EV is typically agreed on an EBITDA basis and is unaffected by this accounting adjustment. However: the equity check (cash needed from PE fund) = EV − Debt + Transaction Costs +/− NWC adjustment. If the NWC target was set based on LIFO inventory, the post-conversion FIFO inventory is $150m higher → the seller receives more for the higher NWC → equity check increases by $150m (net of tax impact = $112.5m effectively, depending on deal structure). This is a real negotiating point in cross-border deals. (c) Year 1–2 P&L: Under FIFO, new purchases flow to COGS at current (higher) prices. In the first sell-through period, COGS reflects the stepped-up PPA inventory value — a one-time COGS increase in Year 1. Subsequently (Year 2+), COGS normalizes to FIFO cost levels. If prices are rising, FIFO COGS is lower than LIFO would have been → gross margins improve vs. old LIFO reporting.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct LIFO→IFRS balance sheet adjustment (inventory +$150m, DTL +$37.5m), (2) equity check impact, (3) Year 1 COGS step-up from inventory at PPA cost, (4) Year 2+ normalization, (5) recognizing this is a deal negotiation item.

questions.question: Using the BCG growth-share matrix framework, describe the expected SCF profile (CFO, CFI, CFF) for each of the four quadrants (Cash Cow, Star, Question Mark, Dog). Explain why understanding this framework is valuable in equity analysis and PE deal selection.
questions.model_answer: Cash Cow (high market share, low growth): High CFO (mature, efficient operations). Low CFI (minimal reinvestment needed — market not growing). Negative CFF (returning cash via dividends and buybacks; repaying debt). Net: strong positive cash generation, mostly returned to shareholders. Star (high market share, high growth): High CFO (market leader, strong unit economics). High CFI outflows (reinvesting to maintain/grow position). Moderate CFF (may issue some debt to fund investment). Net: roughly cash neutral despite profitability. Question Mark (low market share, high growth): Low or negative CFO (early-stage, not yet efficient). High CFI outflows (investing to gain scale). Positive CFF (raising equity/debt to fund the investment). Net: significant cash consumer — requires external funding. Dog (low market share, low growth): Low CFO (poor competitive position, margin pressure). Low or zero CFI (no investment worth making). Variable CFF (may need emergency financing or be harvested). Net: value destruction, exit candidate. Equity analysis value: helps explain why a company's financial position today is either improving or deteriorating — a Question Mark with investor backing can become a Star. A Dog is a dividend cut / restructuring story. PE deal selection: Cash Cows are ideal LBO candidates (high FCF → service debt, return capital). Question Marks are venture/growth equity plays. Dogs are turnarounds (high risk, need operational transformation). Stars require growth equity + patient capital.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct SCF profile for all four quadrants, (2) articulating the logic (why each has that profile), (3) equity analysis application, (4) PE deal type matching.

questions.question: An acquiree's revenue shows a consistent spike in Q4 followed by a decline in Q1. Gross margin improves in Q4 but declines in Q1. DSO spikes at year-end and drops in Q2. AUA coverage is thin. Diagnose what is happening and what additional analyses you would perform in diligence.
questions.model_answer: Diagnosis: Channel stuffing with possible premature revenue recognition. The pattern: Q4 revenue spike (push product to distributors to meet annual targets), Q1 reversal (returns, cancellations, or distributors refuse to reorder until sell-through). Q4 gross margin improvement: either accounting-driven (LIFO liquidation, insufficient returns provision) or real (price increases to Q4 customers). DSO spike at year-end: consistent with recognizing revenue on shipped-not-yet-accepted goods — AR is large because distributors haven't accepted / confirmed the goods yet. Q2 DSO drop: Q4 AR is either collected (real sales) or reversed (returns processed). AUA thin: expected bad debt/returns not adequately provisioned — overstatement of net AR and net income. Analytical steps: (1) Post-period cash collections: how much of Dec 31 AR was collected by Feb 28? If <60%, it's a serious concern. (2) Request monthly shipment vs. sell-through data from distributors: are distributors building inventory (can't absorb shipments)? (3) Return policy: are there formal or informal rights of return for Q4 shipments? Under IFRS 15, revenue cannot be recognized if material return rights exist. (4) Customer-level AR aging: are Q4 debtors the same as Q3, or are new 'customers' appearing only in Q4? (5) Compare QoE-adjusted revenue (excluding Q4 spike) to peer growth rates — what does organic growth look like? (6) Management interviews: what are the sales incentive structures? Are salespeople paid on quarterly shipments or annual collections?
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct diagnosis of channel stuffing, (2) post-period collections as the key test, (3) distributor inventory analysis, (4) IFRS 15 return rights, (5) sales incentive investigation, (6) DSO and AUA interpretation.

questions.question: A PE fund buys a company for 10x EV/EBITDA and sells 5 years later for 12x EV/EBITDA. EBITDA grew from $100m to $160m. Debt fell from $600m to $300m. Identify and explain the sources of equity return. Which value creation lever is most reliable? Which is most risky?
questions.model_answer: Entry: EV = 10 × $100m = $1,000m. Debt = $600m. Equity = $400m. Exit: EV = 12 × $160m = $1,920m. Debt = $300m. Equity = $1,620m. Total equity return = 1,620/400 = 4.05x MOIC (≈ 32% IRR over 5 years). Three sources of equity value creation: (1) EBITDA growth ($100m → $160m = +$60m): at exit 12x multiple, this EBITDA growth adds $60m × 12 = $720m to EV. Contribution to equity = $720m. Most reliable lever: driven by operational improvement (revenue growth, margin expansion, working capital optimization, add-on acquisitions). Management can directly control this. (2) Multiple expansion (10x → 12x): on $160m EBITDA, the 2x multiple expansion adds $160m × 2 = $320m to EV. Riskiest lever: dependent on macro conditions, M&A market sentiment, sector re-rating — entirely outside PE fund's control. PE funds must not rely on multiple expansion in underwriting. If they bought at 10x and sell at 10x (base case), the return is still acceptable if EBITDA grows and debt is repaid. (3) Debt paydown ($600m → $300m = +$300m): every dollar of debt repaid transfers directly to equity. This is the pure financial engineering component — amplifies equity returns mechanically. Reliability is intermediate: driven by FCF (predictable if business is stable), but vulnerable to EBITDA decline (less cash for debt service). Overall: EBITDA growth is the most reliable and most defensible source. Multiple expansion is serendipitous. Debt paydown is mechanical but requires stable operations.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct equity return calculation, (2) correctly identifying and attributing all three value creation levers, (3) EBITDA growth as most reliable, (4) multiple expansion as riskiest, (5) debt paydown as mechanical/reliable but cyclically sensitive.

questions.question: You are an analyst at a PE fund reviewing a first-look financial model for a potential acquisition. Net income CAGR = 15% over 5 years. EBITDA CAGR = 12%. CFO CAGR = 3%. Inventory days: 45→80. DSO: 30→55. DPO: 60→45. Gross margin: 48%→52%. Debt ratio: 25%→55%. Write a one-page investment concern memo to the deal team.
questions.model_answer: INVESTMENT CONCERN MEMO — WORKING CAPITAL AND EARNINGS QUALITY. Summary: While headline NI and EBITDA growth appear attractive, a systematic review of operational metrics reveals significant earnings quality concerns and deteriorating cash generation that require resolution before proceeding. Key Concerns: (1) Cash generation deterioration: NI CAGR 15% vs CFO CAGR 3% over 5 years implies massive accrual accumulation. CRR has likely fallen from near 1.0 to well below 0.5. The business is not converting earnings to cash — this is the single most important concern. (2) Working capital absorption: CCC = DSO + Inventory Days − DPO. CCC entry = 30+45−60 = 15 days. CCC exit = 55+80−45 = 90 days. A 75-day CCC expansion on estimated revenue of $X means the company has absorbed enormous cash in working capital. This explains the NI/CFO gap entirely. (3) Gross margin improvement appears inconsistent: 48%→52% gross margin improvement is positive. But if COGS is understated (LIFO liquidation, NRV write-down avoidance, inventory overstatement), this margin may not be real. Demand full COGS reconciliation. (4) AP compression (DPO: 60→45): Supplier relationships may be deteriorating, or the company is losing negotiating leverage. This is a real cash cost. (5) Leverage increase (Debt ratio 25%→55%): Has debt financed working capital buildup? If so, leverage is funding non-cash earnings — structurally dangerous. Required analyses before proceeding: (1) Full QoE analysis on AR, inventory, and revenue recognition. (2) Post-period collections test. (3) CCC trend decomposition. (4) AUA coverage trend. (5) Supplier payment term review.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) CRR analysis (3% CFO vs 15% NI), (2) correct CCC calculation and expansion, (3) connecting CCC expansion to cash consumption, (4) questioning gross margin quality, (5) DPO deterioration interpretation, (6) structured memo format with clear conclusions and next steps.

questions.question: Professor Novák describes accounting as both a 'map' and a 'maze.' Explain this metaphor fully, give two examples of accounting being a reliable map, two examples of it being a misleading maze, and conclude with how a skilled analyst uses both properties.
questions.model_answer: Map: accounting is standardized and structured — a skilled reader can navigate a set of financial statements and gain genuine understanding of a business. (1) The Balance Sheet reliably shows whether a company is net cash or net debt, current vs. non-current asset structure, and equity vs. debt financing mix. These are factual, verifiable, and consistent across companies. (2) The Statement of Cash Flows — especially CFO — is relatively difficult to manipulate (cash actually changes hands). It reliably shows whether the business generates real cash, regardless of what the IS says. Maze: accounting requires numerous estimates, judgments, and policy choices — and managers have incentives to use this discretion to present the best possible picture (dating game). (1) Goodwill impairment tests: management sets the discount rate and terminal growth assumptions. These can be adjusted within a defensible range to avoid impairment indefinitely — until the business fails. The maze: you cannot see whether goodwill is impaired just by looking at the balance sheet number. (2) Revenue recognition timing for multi-element arrangements (software, long-term contracts): management has significant discretion in identifying performance obligations, estimating standalone selling prices, and determining when control transfers. The same contract can be accounted for very differently by two companies following IFRS 15. Skilled analyst approach: Use the map to build the structural understanding (leverage, asset mix, cash generation capacity). Then probe the maze systematically: CRR, DSO trends, AUA coverage, footnote analysis, accounting policy comparison to peers. The map gives you the questions; the maze investigation gives you confidence in the answers.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) explaining map (standardized, comparable, verifiable), (2) two specific map examples, (3) explaining maze (estimates, judgments, incentives), (4) two specific maze examples, (5) analytical synthesis: use map for structure, probe maze for quality.

questions.question: A B2B company is considering loosening its credit terms (from 30-day to 60-day net) to grow revenue by 15%. Model the working capital impact, analyze whether this is likely to improve ROE, and identify the risks.
questions.model_answer: Working capital impact: Current revenue $1,000m, DSO = 30 days → AR = $1,000m × 30/365 = $82m. Post-change: Revenue = $1,150m (15% growth), DSO = 60 days → AR = $1,150m × 60/365 = $189m. NWC increases by $189m − $82m = $107m. This $107m must be financed (debt, equity, or working capital credit line). ROE analysis: Revenue grows 15%. If gross margin holds, gross profit grows 15%. But: (1) AUA must increase to reflect higher expected bad debts on the new (looser credit quality) customer base. (2) Interest cost on the incremental $107m of AR financing (e.g., at 5% = $5.4m/year) reduces NI. (3) Bad debt expense likely rises as credit quality of new customers is lower than existing. (4) DSO management cost increases (more collections staff, aging complexity). Net NI improvement may be much less than 15% growth implies. For ROE: ROE = NI / Equity. If equity must increase to fund AR (or if debt/interest increases), the ROE improvement is further diluted. At extreme cases (very high bad debt from marginal customers), the policy could reduce ROE despite growing revenue. Risks: (1) Irreversibility — it is very hard to tighten credit terms once loosened (customer expectation is set). (2) Bad debt cascade — in a recession, the marginal customers attracted by easy credit default simultaneously. (3) Working capital spiral — if the company then needs emergency financing to cover the AR pile-up, it loses negotiating power with lenders.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct AR calculation before/after, (2) NWC impact quantification, (3) bad debt expense increase, (4) interest cost of financing AR, (5) ROE impact analysis, (6) irreversibility and recession risk.

questions.question: Two businesses have the same EBITDA margin of 25%. Business A requires $2 of invested capital to generate $1 of revenue. Business B requires $0.50 of invested capital per $1 of revenue. Compare their Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), explain the economic significance, and discuss implications for M&A valuation.
questions.model_answer: ROIC = NOPAT / Invested Capital = EBIT(1-t) / IC. Assuming EBIT margin ≈ 20% (EBITDA 25% minus 5% D&A) and tax 25%: NOPAT margin ≈ 15%. Business A: Revenue $100. IC = $200 (2× revenue). ROIC = $15 / $200 = 7.5%. Business B: Revenue $100. IC = $50 (0.5× revenue). ROIC = $15 / $50 = 30%. Economic significance: Business B generates 30% annual return on every dollar invested — it needs very little capital to grow, meaning it can self-fund growth or return cash to shareholders. Business A needs $2 of capital for every $1 of revenue growth — it must continually reinvest, and if its cost of capital is 10%, its ROIC (7.5%) < WACC → it is destroying value despite the 25% EBITDA margin. ROIC vs. WACC is the true test of value creation: ROIC > WACC = value creation. ROIC < WACC = value destruction, regardless of reported profit. M&A valuation implications: (1) Business B justifies a much higher EV/EBITDA multiple: it generates more FCF per dollar of EBITDA (lower reinvestment needs), so the same EBITDA is 'worth more.' (2) Business A's EBITDA multiple should be lower because the heavy CapEx requirements absorb most of the EBITDA before FCF is available. (3) In an LBO: Business B can carry significant debt (high FCF conversion). Business A will struggle to service debt from limited FCF despite high EBITDA. This is why 'asset-light' businesses trade at premium EBITDA multiples.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct ROIC calculation for both, (2) ROIC vs WACC framework, (3) Business A potentially destroying value despite 25% EBITDA margin, (4) FCF conversion implication, (5) M&A multiple justification (asset-light premium).

questions.question: You paid a 40% premium over the target's pre-announcement share price in an acquisition. Your CFO asks you to justify this premium. Build the complete analytical justification, acknowledging where the premium may have been too high.
questions.model_answer: A 40% acquisition premium is the norm in public M&A (historical average: 25–40%). Analytical justification: (1) Control premium: buyers of 100% of a business pay a premium for control (ability to redirect strategy, cut costs, integrate with acquirer). Control is worth an estimated 15–25% over standalone public market value in most sectors. (2) Synergy value: present value of identified synergies justifies the remainder. At 40% premium on a $1bn EV target = $400m premium to justify. If WACC = 10% and synergies are $50m annual EBITDA benefit, PV of synergies at 10× = $500m → synergies more than justify the premium on paper. (3) Strategic value: access to new markets, technology, talent, or distribution channels that would take years to build organically — valued at NPV of avoided build cost. Where it may have been too high: (1) Revenue synergies are speculative — historically, 40–60% of revenue synergies never materialize. (2) The 'winner's curse': in a competitive auction, the highest bidder is often the most optimistic, not the most informed. Ex-post, auction winners often overpay. (3) Goodwill = premium above net asset value — if it exceeds what synergies can support, goodwill impairment will follow. (4) Management incentives: deal teams are rewarded for closing transactions, creating a bias toward deal completion at any price. Recommendation to CFO: conduct a rigorous annual review comparing actual synergy realization to the deal model within 12 months of closing.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) control premium concept, (2) synergy value calculation, (3) PV framework for synergies, (4) winner's curse acknowledgment, (5) management incentive bias, (6) post-acquisition tracking recommendation.

questions.question: A company has $500m of PPE. Management can choose between a 5-year and a 10-year depreciation life. Walk through the impact of each choice on the IS, BS, SCF, and key ratios (ROA, EBITDA margin, Net Margin, Current Ratio). Which choice would a manager pursuing the dating game prefer?
questions.model_answer: Annual depreciation: 5-year = $100m/year. 10-year = $50m/year. Difference = $50m/year. IS impact: 5-year: EBIT and NI are $50m lower per year (higher D&A). EBITDA is identical (D&A added back). 10-year (dating game choice): EBIT and NI are $50m higher per year. Net margin higher. BS impact: 5-year: Net PPE declines faster (higher accumulated depreciation). Total assets are lower. 10-year: Net PPE stays higher (lower depreciation). Total assets are higher. Retained earnings are higher (lower depreciation expense → higher NI). SCF impact: Identical CFO. D&A is added back in CFO regardless. FCF is identical. Cash flow is completely unaffected by this choice. Key ratios: ROA (NI / Avg Assets): 5-year → lower NI, lower assets. The effect on ROA is ambiguous — depends on relative magnitudes. 10-year → higher NI, higher assets. EBITDA margin: Identical for both (D&A excluded). Net margin: Higher for 10-year choice. Current Ratio: Unaffected (depreciation doesn't involve current assets or liabilities). Dating game preference: 10-year. Higher reported NI, higher EPS, higher ROE (if equity is used in denominator), better-looking IS. The key insight: this is pure accounting choice with ZERO economic effect. The asset depreciates at the same physical rate regardless of the accounting life chosen. An analyst comparing two companies must always check depreciation policy for comparability.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct annual depreciation amounts, (2) IS impact (only D&A-affected metrics), (3) BS impact (net PPE, retained earnings), (4) SCF is identical, (5) EBITDA margin is identical, (6) dating game = 10-year life.

questions.question: Trace $100 of cash through the complete operating cycle of a manufacturer. Show where the $100 appears on the Balance Sheet at each stage, when it hits the Income Statement, and when it returns to the Cash account. Identify all timing discrepancies.
questions.model_answer: Stage 1 — Cash to Raw Materials: $100 cash → $100 Raw Materials inventory. BS: Cash −$100, Inventory +$100. No IS impact yet. Timing discrepancy 1: cash paid before expense recognized (prepayment of production input). Stage 2 — Production (Raw Materials + Labor): Assume $100 raw materials + $30 direct labor → WIP = $130. BS: Raw Materials −$100, WIP +$100, also Wages Payable +$30 (if unpaid), WIP +$30. IS: no impact yet (costs are assets). Timing discrepancy 2: labor cost will be recognized as expense only when goods are sold. Stage 3 — Completion: WIP $130 → Finished Goods $130. BS: WIP −$130, Finished Goods +$130. Stage 4 — Sale on credit (say, sold for $200): Revenue $200 recognized (IS), COGS $130 recognized (IS). BS: Finished Goods −$130, AR +$200, Retained Earnings +$70 (NI). Cash: unchanged. Timing discrepancy 3: revenue recognized before cash received (AR). Stage 5 — Collection: AR $200 → Cash $200. BS: AR −$200, Cash +$200. The $30 labor from Stage 2 is eventually paid: Cash −$30, Wages Payable −$30. Full cycle: $100 cash in → $100 raw materials → production → sold for $200 → $200 cash returned, net gain $70 (minus labor and other costs). The Balance Sheet stores all the timing discrepancies between each stage: inventory, WIP, finished goods, AR are all accruals waiting to convert back to cash.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct BS entries at each stage, (2) identifying when IS impact occurs (only at sale), (3) all three timing discrepancies identified, (4) cash flow timeline, (5) linking back to accrual accounting principle.

questions.question: You are building a comparable company analysis (comps) for a specialty chemicals company. List five adjustments you would make to reported EBITDA and multiples to ensure comparability across companies, and explain the analytical rationale for each.
questions.model_answer: (1) Normalize for one-time items: adjust out restructuring charges, litigation settlements, and write-downs that are not recurring. Rationale: these distort the 'run-rate' EBITDA. However, if a company restructures every 2 years, treat as recurring. (2) Adjust for accounting policy differences: if one company capitalizes R&D and another expenses it, the EBITDA bases are not comparable. Standardize to the same treatment. Similarly, if lease accounting differs (IFRS 16 adoption timing), adjust EBITDA and debt consistently. (3) Remove management fees and related-party costs: PE-owned companies often pay management fees that inflate operating costs and depress EBITDA. Public companies may have owner-operators paying themselves above-market salaries. Normalize to market rates. (4) Adjust for LTM vs NTM: some comps may have already announced revenue guidance changes or completed acquisitions. Use consistent forward/trailing periods and adjust for pre-announced deal synergies. (5) Net of non-controlling interest: for companies with large minority interests, the consolidated EBITDA includes earnings not attributable to the parent. The EV already includes the value of those operations, so the denominator (EBITDA) should also be fully consolidated — but the equity value (numerator of equity multiples) must deduct the MI. Consistent treatment across the peer set is essential. Bonus consideration: seasonality adjustments if companies have different fiscal year-ends that capture different seasonal patterns.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) five distinct adjustments correctly explained, (2) rationale for each connected to comparability, (3) nuanced treatment (not all restructuring is non-recurring), (4) accounting policy standardization, (5) MI treatment.

questions.question: Accounting faces a fundamental tension between relevance (economic substance) and reliability (verifiability). Give three examples where IFRS has chosen relevance over reliability, and three examples where it has chosen reliability. Explain why this tension matters for PE due diligence.
questions.model_answer: Relevance over reliability (equity investor / dating game preference): (1) Fair value accounting (IFRS 13): financial instruments measured at mark-to-market prices. Highly relevant (current economic value) but relies on models for Level 3 assets — potentially subjective and manipulable. (2) Allowance method for bad debts (IFRS 9): estimates expected losses before they are confirmed. More relevant (reflects likely collection) than direct write-off, but requires judgment in setting the allowance. (3) Revenue recognition over time (IFRS 15): recognizing revenue as performance obligations are satisfied, even before cash — more economically meaningful but requires significant judgment on % completion, variable consideration, etc. Reliability over relevance (lender / tax authority preference): (1) Inventory at lower of cost and NRV (IAS 2): using cost (verifiable) as the ceiling. Cannot write up inventory above cost even if market prices rise (more conservative = more reliable). (2) Direct write-off method (only for immaterial amounts): recognizes bad debt only when confirmed — highly verifiable, zero estimates, but recognized too late for matching. (3) Historical cost for PPE (permitted under IAS 16): original cost less depreciation — completely verifiable, no market judgment required, even if current market value is very different. PE due diligence relevance: every area where IFRS chose relevance requires a judgment that management can influence. Due diligence must probe each such area: fair value assumptions, allowance estimates, and revenue recognition policy. The reliability choices are safer — they require less analytical scrutiny. The relevance choices are where the accounting maze lives.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) three relevance examples with correct explanation, (2) three reliability examples, (3) connecting the tension to the dating/begging game, (4) explaining why relevance choices are the due diligence focus.

questions.question: A PE fund buys 75% of a software company for $750m (implying 100% EV = $1,000m). EBITDA = $100m, Net Debt = 0. The minority shareholder retains 25%. Walk through: (a) the entry equity check, (b) the consolidated balance sheet at acquisition, (c) the equity value bridge, and (d) the return calculation at a 5-year exit at 14x EV/EBITDA with EBITDA of $160m.
questions.model_answer: (a) Entry equity check: PE fund pays $750m for 75%. Minority = 25% at fair value = 25/75 × $750m = $250m. Total EV = $1,000m. No debt → equity check = $750m (pure equity, no LBO debt in this example). (b) Consolidated BS at acquisition: Cash decreases by $750m (PE fund's acquisition price). Identifiable assets: PPA assigns assets at fair value (assume = book value for simplicity). Goodwill: Purchase price ($750m) + BV(MI) ($250m implied) − net assets. If net assets = $400m (assumed), Gw = 750+250−400 = $600m (book value MI method). If market value MI = $250m: Gw = 750+250−400 = $600m (same in this case since MI market value = implied proportional). MI = $250m in equity. (c) Equity value bridge at entry: EV = $1,000m. Net Debt = $0. MI = $250m. Equity Value (to majority) = 1,000 − 0 − 250 = $750m ✓ (matches purchase price). (d) Exit: EBITDA = $160m, Multiple = 14x. Exit EV = $2,240m. Assume MI remains 25% on updated equity: Exit equity total = $2,240m (no debt). MI at exit = 25% × $2,240m = $560m. Majority equity = 75% × $2,240m = $1,680m. Return: invested $750m, exit $1,680m = 2.24x MOIC over 5 years ≈ 17.5% IRR. Sources: EBITDA growth $100→$160 (+$60m × 14x = +$840m EV) + multiple expansion 10x→14x on $160m = (+$640m on EBITDA base). No debt paydown since no initial debt.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct equity check, (2) MI in BS equity, (3) correct equity bridge, (4) exit EV and MI deduction, (5) return calculation and source attribution.

questions.question: You have 5 years of financial statements for a consumer company. Describe how you would use both horizontal (trend) and vertical (common-size) analysis to build an investment thesis, and give three specific examples of insights each can provide.
questions.model_answer: Horizontal (trend) analysis: compares each line item across years as % change or indexed to a base year. Insights: (1) Revenue CAGR vs. COGS CAGR — if COGS grows faster than revenue, gross margin is structurally declining (pricing power erosion or input cost inflation). (2) SG&A as trend — flat SG&A with growing revenue signals operating leverage (fixed costs spreading over larger base → EBIT margin expands). Rising SG&A-to-revenue signals investment phase or cost control failure. (3) Net income vs. CFO divergence over 5 years — if NI CAGR outpaces CFO CAGR, accruals have been building systematically. This is the most powerful horizontal signal in the data. Vertical (common-size) analysis: each line item as % of Net Sales in each year. Insights: (1) Gross margin % trend — is the business's core pricing power stable, improving, or declining? Gross margin is the most stable indicator of competitive position. (2) SG&A % trend — is the cost structure changing? Rising SG&A% may mean the company is investing in brand/sales force (positive) or losing efficiency (negative). (3) Peer comparison: applying the same common-size template to competitors reveals structural differences — one company's 52% gross margin vs. peer's 38% signals genuinely different business models (higher value-added product, stronger brand, proprietary distribution). Combined use: horizontal shows direction and velocity of change. Vertical shows structural proportions. Together, they allow building an investment narrative: 'gross margin has expanded 400bps over 5 years (vertical) while COGS has grown at only 80% of revenue growth (horizontal) — indicating pricing power and scale benefits.'
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct definition of both methods, (2) three specific horizontal insights, (3) three specific vertical insights, (4) example of combined use in investment narrative.

questions.question: During M&A due diligence on a food manufacturer, you discover: (a) inventory has grown 40% while COGS grew 10%, (b) there have been no NRV write-downs in 3 years despite known commodity price declines, (c) the company switched from FIFO to average cost last year. What are your concerns and what are the deal implications?
questions.model_answer: (a) Inventory growing 40% vs COGS 10%: inventory days have expanded dramatically. Possible explanations: (1) Deliberate stockpiling ahead of anticipated price increases (benign but speculative). (2) Slow-moving or obsolete inventory accumulating — product lines in decline, demand forecasting failures. (3) Revenue recognition manipulation — goods being held as 'inventory' that should have been expensed as returns. Deal implication: request full aging and SKU-level inventory analysis. Identify what % is >180 days old. Any inventory not expected to sell within 12 months should be written down as a deal adjustment. (b) No NRV write-downs despite commodity price declines: this is a classic reliability red flag. Under IAS 2, inventory must be written down to NRV if market prices fall below cost. 3 years without write-downs despite known price declines = potential inventory overstatement. Calculate: if commodity X is 30% of COGS, and market price has fallen 20%, NRV write-down should be approximately $X×30%×20% = material amount. Deal implication: independently estimate required NRV write-down and reduce EBITDA accordingly as a QoE adjustment. At 10x multiple, even a $5m write-down = $50m of EV impact. (c) FIFO to Average Cost switch: this is an accounting policy change that must be disclosed and retrospectively applied (IAS 8). The key question: was this change made to improve, reduce, or normalize reported margins? If prices are falling, AC gives lower COGS than FIFO — possible margin improvement motivation. If prices are rising, vice versa. Request the retrospective restatement to understand the P&L impact over 5 years under each method. Consider normalizing EBITDA to one consistent method for the deal valuation.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) inventory days calculation and implication, (2) NRV write-down obligation under IAS 2, (3) QoE adjustment calculation, (4) accounting policy change red flag (IAS 8 restatement), (5) concrete deal implications for each finding.

questions.question: You are projecting FCF for an LBO target over a 5-year hold period. Revenue is expected to grow 8% annually. EBITDA margin is stable at 22%. D&A = 4% of revenue. CapEx = 5% of revenue. NWC = 15% of revenue. Tax rate 25%. Build the Year 1 FCF starting from Year 0 revenue of $500m and explain the model logic.
questions.model_answer: Year 0 Revenue: $500m. Year 1 Revenue: $500m × 1.08 = $540m. Year 1 EBITDA: $540m × 22% = $118.8m. Year 1 D&A: $540m × 4% = $21.6m. Year 1 EBIT: $118.8m − $21.6m = $97.2m. Year 1 NOPAT (taxes on EBIT): $97.2m × (1 − 25%) = $72.9m. Year 1 D&A add-back: +$21.6m. Year 1 CapEx: −$540m × 5% = −$27m. Year 1 ΔNWC: NWC Year 0 = $500m × 15% = $75m. NWC Year 1 = $540m × 15% = $81m. ΔNWC = +$6m (NWC increased, cash absorbed) → −$6m in FCF. Year 1 FCF = $72.9m + $21.6m − $27m − $6m = $61.5m. FCF conversion: $61.5m / $118.8m EBITDA = 51.8%. Model logic: (1) Revenue drives everything via the % of revenue assumptions. (2) NOPAT = EBIT × (1-t) captures the tax-adjusted operating return. (3) D&A is added back (non-cash) then CapEx is subtracted (real cash). (4) ΔNWC captures cash absorbed by working capital growth — in a growing business, NWC grows proportionally, requiring cash investment each year. (5) CapEx > D&A ($27m > $21.6m) → growth CapEx is present, consistent with an 8% growth company. If CapEx = D&A, it would imply pure maintenance — no net new capacity.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct Year 1 revenue, (2) EBITDA, EBIT, NOPAT calculation, (3) correct ΔNWC (not absolute NWC), (4) correct FCF = $61.5m, (5) FCF conversion analysis, (6) model logic explanation.

questions.question: An acquirer pays $2,000m for a target with book value of assets of $800m, liabilities of $300m, and fair value of assets of $1,100m. Identify the components of goodwill, explain what each represents economically, and discuss the post-acquisition financial statement impacts over 5 years.
questions.model_answer: BV Net Assets = $800m − $300m = $500m. FV Net Assets = $1,100m − $300m = $800m. Purchase price = $2,000m. Goodwill decomposition: (1) Tangible asset step-up: $1,100m − $800m = $300m (e.g., PPE revalued from $800m to $1,100m book). This represents the market value of physical assets exceeding their depreciated historical cost — real estate appreciation, machinery with residual value above book. (2) Identifiable intangibles (off-BS): assume PPA identifies $500m of intangibles: brand $200m, customer relationships $200m, technology $100m. These were not on the target's BS (internally developed → can't recognize under IFRS 38 standalone). But in M&A they are identifiable → recognized. FV Net Assets now = $800m + $500m = $1,300m. (3) Residual goodwill: $2,000m − $1,300m = $700m. This represents synergies, assembled workforce, strategic premium, and unidentifiable value. Post-acquisition financial statement impacts: Year 1–5 IS: (1) Higher D&A from step-up: $300m tangible revaluation over remaining life (say 15 years) = $20m/year additional depreciation. (2) Intangible amortization: brand $200m (indefinite life — not amortized under IFRS); customer relationships $200m/10 years = $20m/year; technology $100m/5 years = $20m/year. Total additional amortization = $40m/year. (3) Goodwill ($700m) — no annual charge; tested for impairment. Total additional annual D&A charge: $20m + $40m = $60m. NI is reduced by $60m × (1-25%) = $45m per year. EBITDA is unaffected (D&A added back). BS: intangibles decline as amortized; goodwill constant unless impaired.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct three-layer goodwill decomposition, (2) economic explanation of each layer, (3) tangible step-up D&A, (4) each intangible amortization life and calculation, (5) EBITDA immunity, (6) NI impact.

questions.question: A PE fund's portfolio company has CCC of 95 days. Industry peers average 45 days. The CEO argues this is because 'our business is different.' What do you say back? How do you analyze the gap, and what are realistic improvement levers?
questions.model_answer: The CEO's response is the classic resistance to operational challenge. The correct analytical response: 'Tell me specifically which component of the CCC (DSO, inventory days, DPO) is different, and explain the business reason with data. Not assertions.' Decompose the gap: Assume CCC = DSO 50 + Inventory 70 − DPO 25 = 95 days vs. peer CCC = DSO 30 + Inventory 45 − DPO 30 = 45 days. Each component gap: DSO gap = 20 days → on $500m revenue, this is $500m × 20/365 = $27m of cash tied up. Investigate: longer payment terms to customers vs. peers? Or collection efficiency problem? Inventory gap = 25 days → on $200m COGS, this is $200m × 25/365 = $14m. Investigate: product complexity, safety stock policy, demand forecasting accuracy. DPO gap = −5 days (paying faster than peers) → on $200m COGS, $200m × 5/365 = $2.7m additional cash. Investigate: missing supplier negotiation leverage or supplier incentive agreements. 'Our business is different' is valid IF: (1) DSO is higher because customers are genuinely large enterprises with 90-day standard terms that cannot be changed without losing business. (2) Inventory is higher due to regulatory requirements (pharmaceutical safety stock). (3) DPO is lower because supplier contracts have early payment incentives that generate positive economics. It is NOT valid if these are simply operational failures. Improvement levers: (1) AR factoring or supply chain financing (instant DSO improvement). (2) SKU rationalization (cut slow-moving products). (3) Dynamic forecasting to reduce safety stock. (4) AP payment term renegotiation. Quantify the prize: 50-day CCC improvement on $500m revenue = $500m × 50/365 = $68m one-time cash release.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) decomposing CCC into components to isolate the gap, (2) quantifying cash tied up per component, (3) distinguishing legitimate business reasons from operational failure, (4) at least three specific improvement levers, (5) total cash release quantification.

questions.question: Explain why an equity investor and a bank lender looking at the same company would focus on fundamentally different accounting metrics. Give three specific metrics for each, explaining the preference.
questions.model_answer: Equity investor (relevance-first, dating game): earns a residual claim — the upside above all fixed obligations. Cares about: (1) EBITDA / EBIT margin and growth — measures underlying business value creation. The higher and more consistently growing, the more valuable the equity. (2) ROE and ROIC — how much value is generated per dollar of equity invested? These are the ultimate measures of management efficiency and pricing power. (3) FCF per share / earnings quality — is the reported profit converting to real cash? Equity valuation models are fundamentally discounted cash flow models. Accrual NI is only useful as a proxy for FCF — equity investors probe whether the proxy holds. Bank lender (reliability-first, begging game): earns a fixed return (interest). Does not benefit from upside but bears full downside below covenant thresholds. Cares about: (1) Debt / EBITDA — can the company repay the loan within a reasonable period (typically 5–7 years)? This is the primary leverage test in leveraged finance. (2) EBITDA / Interest (TIE / Interest Coverage) — will the company generate enough operating cash to pay interest every period? Covenant breach triggers default rights. (3) Current Ratio and Quick Ratio / short-term liquidity — will the company have enough liquid assets to meet obligations as they come due? In a workout scenario, the lender's recovery depends on liquidation value, not going-concern EBITDA. This explains why IFRS (equity investor focused) leans toward relevance, while tax authorities and bank covenants lean toward reliability.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correctly characterizing equity investor (residual claimant, upside-focused) vs lender (fixed return, downside-focused), (2) three equity metrics correctly explained, (3) three lender metrics correctly explained, (4) connecting to relevance/reliability tension.

questions.question: You acquire a company that has $200m of AR, $8m of AUA, and you identify during due diligence that: (a) actual historical bad debt rate is 8–10% of gross AR, (b) $30m of AR is >180 days overdue, (c) the largest customer (25% of AR = $50m) has just announced bankruptcy. What is the adjusted net AR, the QoE EBITDA adjustment, and the impact on deal price?
questions.model_answer: Gross AR = $200m. AUA as reported = $8m (4% coverage). Required AUA calculation: (1) Customer bankruptcy: $50m is likely fully uncollectible. AUA needed for this customer alone = $50m × 90% (assume 10% recovery in bankruptcy) = $45m. (2) >180 days overdue: $30m at, say, 80% expected loss = $24m (this includes the bankrupt customer if they are in the overdue bucket, avoid double-counting). Let's say $30m overdue excludes bankrupt customer → AUA for overdue = $24m. (3) Remaining AR: $200m − $50m (bankrupt) − $30m (overdue) = $120m at historical 6% rate (lower end since normal) = $7.2m. Total required AUA = $45m + $24m + $7.2m = $76.2m. Existing AUA = $8m. Required adjustment = $76.2m − $8m = $68.2m additional provision. Adjusted Net AR = $200m − $76.2m = $123.8m (vs. reported $192m). QoE EBITDA adjustment: the $68.2m additional bad debt expense would reduce EBITDA by $68.2m (one-time, non-recurring if this is genuinely an isolated event). However: (1) If the AUA was systematically underprovided over several years, some portion is a recurring annual QoE adjustment. (2) In an LBO, the $68.2m excess provision is typically treated as a BS adjustment (reduce NWC target by $68.2m → reduce equity check). Deal price impact: at 10x EV/EBITDA, if any portion is treated as recurring EBITDA adjustment, deal price falls by 10× that amount. BS-only treatment: equity check decreases by $68.2m directly (lower NWC at closing).
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) identifying insufficient AUA, (2) correct layered AUA calculation, (3) adjusted net AR calculation, (4) QoE treatment (recurring vs. one-time), (5) deal price impact via NWC adjustment or EBITDA multiple.

questions.question: A PE-backed company reports a P/E ratio of 35x on listing (IPO). A comparable non-PE company in the same sector lists at 22x P/E. The PE company has higher EBITDA margins. Is the PE company genuinely more valuable per dollar of earnings, or could accounting explain this difference?
questions.model_answer: The premium P/E for the PE-backed company deserves scrutiny. Several accounting-driven explanations: (1) PPA amortization: the PE-backed company absorbed significant PPA charges from the original LBO (amortizing acquired intangibles). These charges have been depressing NI for years. By IPO (say, 5 years post-LBO), many intangibles are fully amortized → NI suddenly jumps (lower D&A). The 35x P/E is on a depressed-then-recovering NI base, not a permanently higher earnings power. (2) Debt paydown: at LBO entry, significant debt created high interest expense → low NI. By IPO, most debt is repaid → NI is much higher. P/E is high because NI has just normalized upward. (3) EBITDA margin illusion: higher reported EBITDA can be partly QoE-adjusted (one-time add-backs, normalization of owner costs) that inflated the equity story but don't reflect continuing economics. (4) Accounting policy choices: if the PE fund made favorable accounting choices (longer depreciation lives, optimistic revenue recognition) during the hold period to maximize exit value. True value assessment: (1) Compare EV/EBITDA multiples instead of P/E — removes the financing and amortization distortions. (2) Compare FCF multiples — actual cash generation per dollar invested. (3) Normalize NI for the year of IPO (remove one-time PPA unwind effects). (4) Look at 3-year forward NI projections to assess whether the current earnings level is sustainable. The higher EBITDA margin is likely real (PE operational improvements). The premium P/E is partly accounting and partly genuine value.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) PPA amortization completing → NI jump at IPO, (2) debt paydown effect on NI/P/E, (3) recommendation to use EV/EBITDA instead of P/E, (4) FCF multiple as alternative, (5) acknowledging that some premium may be real (PE improvements).

questions.question: A company reports three years of strong CFO growth. In Year 4, CFO drops 60% despite flat revenues. Subsequent diligence reveals a large acquisition was made in Year 3 and fully consolidated in Year 4. Explain all the mechanisms by which the consolidation of an acquired company could reduce CFO, and what this means for valuation.
questions.model_answer: Consolidation begins in the year of acquisition (or when control is gained). In Year 4 (first full year of consolidation), CFO can appear to drop due to: (1) Target's NWC profile: if the acquired company has a less efficient working capital structure (higher DSO, higher inventory days, lower DPO) than the parent, consolidating 100% of its working capital drags the group's CFO. The NWC build from the target flows through Year 4 CFO as incremental AR, inventory increases. (2) Integration costs: integration-related cash costs (redundancy payments, system migration, consulting fees) appear in CFO but are labeled 'one-time' by management. These real cash costs are often buried in CFO and not separately disclosed. (3) Transaction-related AR and deferred revenue: the target may have unusual year-end receivables patterns or deferred revenue that unwinds in Year 4. (4) Interest payments increase: if the acquisition was debt-financed and IFRS classifies interest paid as CFO, the additional interest payments reduce CFO significantly in Year 4. (5) Working capital normalization: if the target held excess payables pre-sale (artificially high DPO to look cash-generative), these unwind post-acquisition as the PE fund's standard payment terms are applied. Valuation implications: (1) Year 4 CFO is not representative of steady-state performance — must normalize for all of the above. (2) CRR in Year 4 will look terrible (low CFO vs. consolidated NI) — but this may be transitional. (3) In modeling Year 5+ FCF, the question is: does working capital stabilize at the combined level, or is there further integration-related cash absorption?
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) target NWC drag on consolidated CFO, (2) integration cash costs in CFO, (3) interest expense increase (if IFRS CFO treatment), (4) working capital normalization, (5) valuation implication (Year 4 CFO is not representative).

questions.question: You have 30 minutes before an IB deal team meeting to review a manufacturing company. Key data: Revenue $800m (flat for 3 years). Gross margin 38% (was 44% three years ago). EBITDA $72m (was $120m). NWC $180m (was $90m). Net Debt $450m (was $200m). Goodwill $300m (unchanged). ROE 4%. DSO: 35→65 days. Inventory Days: 45→90 days. Write the key talking points for the meeting.
questions.model_answer: MANUFACTURING CO — PRELIMINARY INVESTMENT ASSESSMENT. 1. Core profitability collapse: EBITDA has fallen from $120m to $72m (-40%) on flat revenues.
