This is structural, not cyclical — flat revenues mean no volume decline explains it. Gross margin compression (44%→38% = -600bps) is the primary driver. Likely causes: input cost inflation not passed through pricing, product mix deterioration, or COGS manipulation (recommend COGS decomposition). 2. Working capital crisis: NWC has doubled ($90m→$180m) despite flat revenues. CCC has expanded dramatically: DSO +30 days (AR building — possible revenue quality issue, collection failure, or customer stress). Inventory Days +45 days (demand weakness, obsolescence, or overstocking). Combined NWC drag = approximately $90m of cash absorbed — this directly explains why debt has increased (the company has been borrowing to fund working capital). 3. Leverage escalation: Net Debt $200m→$450m with EBITDA falling. Leverage has gone from 1.7x to 6.25x Debt/EBITDA — approaching distress territory. With $72m EBITDA and, say, $27m interest (6% on $450m), TIE = 72m EBIT / 27m ≈ 2.7x — fragile. Any further EBITDA decline risks covenant breach. 4. Goodwill concern: $300m goodwill unchanged for 3 years during which EBITDA fell 40%. This should have triggered impairment. The absence of any impairment charge is highly suspicious — likely an accounting quality issue. At $72m EBITDA and a 10x sector multiple, the business is worth $720m. Net debt = $450m, goodwill = $300m. If goodwill carries at $300m but recoverable value is impaired, a large write-down is coming. 5. ROE of 4% on a 10%+ cost of equity = value destruction. This business requires immediate operational intervention on: (a) pricing/COGS, (b) working capital discipline, (c) goodwill write-down preparation.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) EBITDA decline source analysis (gross margin), (2) NWC diagnosis with DSO and inventory components, (3) leverage ratio calculation, (4) TIE calculation and covenant risk, (5) goodwill impairment flag, (6) ROE vs. cost of capital, (7) structured talking points format.

questions.question: Explain how a company can increase its EPS without improving its underlying business. Give three specific mechanisms and explain why each is potentially misleading.
questions.model_answer: (1) Share buybacks: EPS = NI / Shares Outstanding. If the company buys back shares using debt (debt-funded buyback), NI falls slightly (higher interest expense) but shares outstanding fall much more, mechanically increasing EPS. The business is no better — it has just taken on more risk (more debt) to reduce the denominator. Misleading because: ROE and ROIC are unimproved; the leverage increase creates future fragility. (2) Depreciation life extension: increase PPE useful life (e.g., from 10 to 15 years). Annual D&A decreases → NI increases → EPS increases. Zero economic impact. Cash flow unchanged. But EPS improves. Misleading because: EBITDA and FCF are identical — EPS growth is pure accounting policy choice. (3) Acquisition accretion: acquire a company at below-P/E cost of capital. If the acquirer's P/E is 25x and it acquires a company at 12x P/E (using debt), the acquired earnings, net of interest cost, add more to NI than the interest reduces it → EPS 'accretion.' Misleading because: EPS accretion ignores whether the acquisition creates economic value (ROIC vs. WACC analysis). Many accretive acquisitions have destroyed shareholder value. PE investors focus on FCF per share and ROIC, not EPS, for this reason.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) buyback mechanism correctly explained, (2) depreciation policy correctly explained, (3) acquisition accretion correctly explained, (4) clear explanation of why each is misleading, (5) FCF/ROIC as superior metrics.

questions.topic: FIFO, LIFO, and the Tax Game
questions.question: A US company is considering switching from FIFO to LIFO in an inflationary environment. Walk through all the financial statement and tax implications, and explain why the decision is not straightforward despite the apparent tax benefit.
questions.model_answer: In an inflationary environment, LIFO vs. FIFO differences: IS: LIFO COGS > FIFO COGS → lower pre-tax income → lower current tax payment. BS: LIFO inventory < FIFO inventory (older cheap prices retained) → lower total assets. Tax benefit: lower taxable income × tax rate. On $50m LIFO reserve at 25% tax = $12.5m cash tax saved cumulatively. Why the decision is not straightforward: (1) LIFO conformity rule: switching to LIFO for tax purposes requires using LIFO for financial reporting too. This lowers reported gross margins and NI. If the company has debt covenants based on net income or equity (common), the lower LIFO net income could breach covenants. (2) Lower reported earnings affect bonus targets, PE valuation multiples, and equity analyst estimates — management may resist. (3) The LIFO reserve is a deferred tax liability: if prices ever fall, or if the company is acquired (IFRS conversion), the LIFO reserve must be unwound, creating a large taxable gain — the tax benefit is not permanent, only deferred. (4) If inventory quantities decline (LIFO liquidation), old cheap layers force low COGS in a bad year — creating volatile margins. (5) International comparability: LIFO is not permitted under IFRS. If the company is acquired by a European entity, LIFO must be unwound, creating a tax event at exactly the wrong time (in a deal). Conclusion: the tax savings are real but deferred and conditional. The financial reporting cost, covenant risk, and deal complexity often outweigh the benefit.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct tax benefit calculation, (2) LIFO conformity rule, (3) covenant impact, (4) LIFO reserve as deferred tax liability (not permanent savings), (5) LIFO liquidation risk, (6) IFRS acquisition complication.

questions.question: A company generates $200m of FCF annually. Management proposes three uses: (a) $100m in organic growth CapEx, (b) $60m in acquisitions, (c) $40m returned to shareholders via dividends. As a PE investor, how would you evaluate each allocation, and what framework do you apply?
questions.model_answer: Framework: Capital allocation should be evaluated by the expected ROIC of each use vs. WACC. Capital that earns above WACC creates value; below WACC destroys value. (a) Organic growth CapEx ($100m): Questions: What is the expected return on this investment? Build a mini-DCF: if CapEx generates $20m of incremental NOPAT annually at WACC of 10%, NPV = $200m terminal value − $100m outlay = $100m value creation. If ROIC on organic growth is 20% (> WACC 10%) → excellent allocation. The PE test: require management to present ROIC projections for each organic investment. High-ROIC organic growth is the most value-creating allocation. (b) Acquisitions ($60m): Scrutinize harder. What synergies are being assumed? At what multiple? An acquisition at 15x EBITDA for a 10x WACC business destroys value unless synergies close the gap. PE instinct: acquisitions above the company's own trading multiple are value-neutral at best (paying up for earnings you could otherwise create organically). Require a post-investment review of past acquisitions — is management a good acquirer? (c) Return to shareholders ($40m via dividends): Dividends are value-neutral in theory (Modigliani-Miller). However: if management cannot find above-WACC investments for the remaining $40m, returning it is the correct decision. A buyback might be preferred over dividend if shares trade below intrinsic value (buyback creates value; dividend is flat). Key principle: excess FCF that cannot be deployed above WACC should be returned. A company that hoards cash or invests at sub-WACC returns is destroying value even if it's generating FCF.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) ROIC vs WACC framework stated, (2) organic CapEx evaluation (ROIC required), (3) acquisition scrutiny (synergies, multiple), (4) return to shareholders as default for excess capital, (5) dividend vs buyback choice, (6) connected to value creation principles.

questions.question: MajorCo owns 60% of SubCo, which owns 80% of GrandChildCo. Explain how consolidation works at each level, who is consolidated into whose accounts, and how minority interests arise at each level.
questions.model_answer: Two-level consolidation hierarchy: Level 1 — SubCo into MajorCo: MajorCo owns 60% of SubCo → SubCo is a subsidiary (>50% control). MajorCo consolidates 100% of SubCo's assets and liabilities. Non-Controlling Interest (NCI) at Level 1: 40% of SubCo's net assets (and income) belongs to external shareholders → recognized as NCI in MajorCo's consolidated equity. Level 2 — GrandChildCo into SubCo: SubCo owns 80% of GrandChildCo → GrandChildCo is SubCo's subsidiary. SubCo consolidates 100% of GrandChildCo's assets and liabilities. NCI at Level 2: 20% of GrandChildCo's net assets belongs to GrandChildCo's external shareholders → recognized as NCI in SubCo's accounts. When MajorCo consolidates SubCo, it brings in 100% of SubCo's consolidated accounts (which already include 100% of GrandChildCo). So in MajorCo's group accounts: 100% of GrandChildCo's assets appear. GrandChildCo's 20% NCI appears as a minority (GrandChildCo NCI). SubCo's 40% NCI appears as a minority (SubCo NCI). MajorCo's effective economic interest in GrandChildCo = 60% × 80% = 48% — less than majority, yet GrandChildCo is fully consolidated because control exists at every level. Valuation bridge: In the EV-to-equity bridge, MajorCo must subtract BOTH minority interests (SubCo NCI and GrandChildCo NCI) to arrive at the equity value attributable to MajorCo shareholders. This creates complexity in consolidation — and explains why cascading minority interests are a significant complication in M&A structuring and valuation.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct identification of both subsidiary relationships (>50% = consolidation), (2) Level 1 NCI (40% of SubCo), (3) Level 2 NCI (20% of GrandChildCo), (4) effective economic interest calculation (48%), (5) both NCIs in the equity bridge.

questions.question: An LBO uses $400m of equity and $600m of debt to acquire a $1,000m EV business. Trace the impact on all three financial statements at acquisition, at the end of Year 1 (EBITDA $120m, D&A $20m, CapEx $25m, debt repaid $30m), and identify the key financial metrics an LBO lender would monitor.
questions.model_answer: At acquisition — Balance Sheet: Assets (from PPA) $1,000m, Goodwill (assume $200m), Total Assets $1,200m. Liabilities: Debt $600m. Equity: $400m. Checks: $600m + $400m ≠ $1,200m — gap of $200m is goodwill above net assets → I need to model this correctly: EV = $1,000m = Purchase price for net assets. If FV net assets = $800m, Goodwill = $200m. BS: Assets $800m + Goodwill $200m = $1,000m total; Debt $600m + Equity $400m = $1,000m ✓. At acquisition — SCF: CFI: −$1,000m (acquisition). CFF: +$600m debt raised + $400m equity raised. Net cash from deal transactions = 0 (cash in = cash out). Year 1 — IS: EBIT = $120m − $20m = $100m. Interest = $600m × 6% = $36m (assumed rate). Pre-tax = $64m. Tax 25% = $16m. NI = $48m. Year 1 — BS changes: Retained Earnings +$48m. Debt −$30m → Debt = $570m. PPE net = −$20m D&A + $25m CapEx = +$5m. Cash: per SCF. Year 1 — SCF: CFO = NI $48m + D&A $20m (no WC change assumed) = $68m. CFI: −$25m CapEx. CFF: −$36m interest (if CFO classification) or classified CFF; −$30m debt repayment → CFF net = −$30m (plus interest treatment). Net cash: $68m − $25m − $30m = $13m cash increase. Key lender metrics: (1) Debt/EBITDA: $570m/$120m = 4.75x (entry 5.0x → now 4.75x → good trajectory). (2) Interest Coverage (TIE): $100m/$36m = 2.8x (minimum covenant typically 2.0x). (3) FCF for debt service: $68m − $25m = $43m FCF → can service $30m repayment + $36m interest = $66m total service ($43m < $66m: need cash sweeps or PIK — model problem). (4) Leverage step-down schedule: is debt falling faster than EBITDA declines?
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) correct acquisition BS, (2) Year 1 IS with interest, (3) correct CFO + CFI + CFF Year 1, (4) Debt/EBITDA calculation, (5) TIE calculation, (6) FCF vs. debt service coverage — identifying the potential issue.

questions.question: You are reviewing a company that has restated its financials three times in five years. Each restatement related to revenue recognition. The CFO was replaced twice. Describe your analytical approach, the specific tests you would perform, and the implications for deal structuring if you proceed.
questions.model_answer: Red alert: three revenue recognition restatements + two CFO changes = systemic governance failure, not isolated accounting errors. Analytical approach: (1) Understand the pattern: what exactly was restated each time? Was revenue being pulled forward (Q4 into Q3), inflated with fictitious customers, or misclassified (gross vs. net)? The specific mechanism reveals whether the problem is systemic culture or manageable policy failure. (2) Board and audit committee review: did the board know? Was there whistleblower activity? If the audit committee was involved or complicit, the governance failure is terminal. (3) Independent expert review: commission an independent forensic accountant to re-examine all revenue from the current period forward from scratch. Do not rely on management-prepared numbers. (4) Post-period cash collections: test every current AR balance for cash receipt. Any revenue that does not eventually convert to cash was likely fictitious or premature. (5) Customer confirmation letters: contact the top 20 customers directly to confirm the amounts owed and the nature of the relationship. (6) Contract review: read every significant contract to assess whether the performance obligation was truly satisfied at the time revenue was recognized. Implications for deal structuring if proceeding: (1) Increased reps and warranties insurance scope — require seller to hold back significant escrow to cover potential future restatements. (2) Earnout structure: make part of the purchase price contingent on Year 1–2 post-close audited revenue confirming the historical revenue trend. (3) Lower entry multiple: the governance/accounting risk warrants a discount vs. a clean target — perhaps 1–2x EBITDA lower. (4) Enhanced financial monitoring: monthly reporting, CFO approval by buyer, independent auditor with direct relationship to acquirer. (5) MAC clause: ensure the purchase agreement includes a material adverse change clause that allows walkaway if another restatement occurs.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) characterizing as governance failure not accounting error, (2) post-period cash collections test, (3) customer confirmations, (4) independent forensic review, (5) earnout structure, (6) escrow and enhanced monitoring.

questions.question: In an M&A deal, the NWC target is a key negotiating point between buyer and seller. The seller argues NWC = AR + Inventory − AP = $80m as the target. The buyer argues NWC should be $55m based on a 12-month average. Both parties use the company's own financials. How can both be right? What is the correct framework?
questions.model_answer: Both can be justified by different legitimate interpretations of the same data. Why seller prefers $80m (likely year-end balance): (1) The business may be seasonal — if it is a Q4-heavy consumer business, year-end NWC is genuinely elevated (high pre-season inventory, high AR from Q4 sales not yet collected). (2) The $80m may be the amount needed to operate the business at peak (which happens to be Q4 when the deal is closing). Using $80m as the target means the buyer pays for peak working capital, which is appropriate if the business genuinely needs it. Why buyer prefers $55m (12-month average): (1) The 12-month average smooths seasonal peaks and represents the 'normal' level of NWC needed to run the business. (2) If NWC is $80m at closing but typically $55m at other times, the buyer would receive $25m of 'excess' NWC — artificially inflating the purchase price if the seller's target is $80m. Correct framework: (1) Determine whether the business is genuinely seasonal. Plot NWC month-by-month over 2–3 years. (2) NWC target should equal the normalized NWC needed to operate the business at the acquired revenue run-rate. For seasonal businesses: typically 12-month average is used; for non-seasonal, trailing 3-month average at closing is reasonable. (3) Specifically exclude: cash (separate debt bridge item), short-term debt (financing item), deferred revenue that is not truly an operational liability. (4) The peg should be negotiated, with clear definitions of what's included, and backed by monthly data. Deal mechanics: if closing NWC > target → seller gets a dollar-for-dollar payment from buyer. If closing NWC < target → buyer receives a dollar-for-dollar payment from seller.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) explaining why both numbers can be valid (seasonality), (2) 12-month average vs. closing balance comparison, (3) correct NWC items (operating only, exclude cash and debt), (4) dollar-for-dollar adjustment mechanics, (5) monthly data as the resolution.

questions.question: Walk through the complete equity value bridge from Enterprise Value to equity value per share. Include every adjustment, explain the rationale for each, and give an example where each adjustment could be significant.
questions.model_answer: Enterprise Value = EBITDA × Multiple (or DCF-based). EV represents the total cost to acquire 100% of the business irrespective of capital structure. Bridge to Equity Value: (1) Less: Net Debt (Debt minus Cash). Rationale: debt is a prior claim — equity holders receive the residual. Example of significance: a highly leveraged company (5x Debt/EBITDA) can have $2bn EV but only $200m equity value — debt absorbs most of the enterprise. (2) Less: Minority Interest. Rationale: EV includes 100% of consolidated operations including subsidiaries with NCI. Equity holders of the parent don't own the NCI portion. Example: a company with a 40% minority in a major subsidiary — NCI may represent $500m, significantly reducing equity value. (3) Less: Preferred Stock. Rationale: preferred stock has a liquidation preference over common equity. Common equity holders receive the residual below preferred. Example: VC-backed companies often have large preferred stock stacks that nearly consume the entire equity value in sale. (4) Less: Pension Deficit (Underfunded Pension). Rationale: a pension deficit is an obligation to fund retirees — economically equivalent to debt. Example: legacy industrial companies may have $1bn+ pension deficits that must be deducted. (5) Less: Earn-out obligations / deferred consideration. Rationale: future payments owed to sellers are economic liabilities. Example: a recent acquisition with $100m earnout if targets are met. (6) Plus/Minus: Operating lease obligations (post-IFRS 16, typically already in debt). (7) Divide by diluted shares outstanding. Equity Value per Share = Equity Value / Diluted Shares (including options, warrants, convertibles on treasury stock method). Each item in the bridge can swing equity value by hundreds of millions — why deal teams spend enormous time mapping each item before signing.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) starting from EV, (2) each deduction with rationale, (3) specific real-world example for each, (4) diluted shares for per-share calculation, (5) explanation of why each item can be material.

questions.question: You are given these two sets of ratios for two identical-size companies in the same industry. Company A: Gross margin 45%, DSO 35 days, Inventory days 40 days, DPO 60 days, Debt/EBITDA 1.5x, ROE 22%. Company B: Gross margin 42%, DSO 65 days, Inventory days 80 days, DPO 30 days, Debt/EBITDA 4.0x, ROE 22%. Write a comparative analysis and PE investment recommendation.
questions.model_answer: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS — COMPANIES A AND B. Both have identical ROE of 22%. The DuPont analysis reveals very different underlying quality. Company A profile: (1) Superior gross margin (45% vs 42%) — better pricing power or lower COGS. (2) Excellent working capital: CCC = 35+40−60 = 15 days. Negative-almost CCC means the company is funded by its own operating cycle. NWC is minimal → requires little invested capital. (3) Low leverage (1.5x Debt/EBITDA) — resilient balance sheet, covenant headroom, capacity for acquisition debt. (4) ROE of 22% driven by operational excellence + modest leverage. Company B profile: (1) Lower gross margin — weaker competitive position. (2) Deteriorated working capital: CCC = 65+80−30 = 115 days vs. A's 15 days = 100-day gap. This represents massive cash tied up in operations, requiring more capital (or more debt) to fund. (3) High leverage (4.0x Debt/EBITDA) — the debt is financing Company B's working capital inefficiency. ROE appears identical to A only because high leverage mechanically inflates ROE via the equity multiplier. (4) In a revenue decline: Company B's cash cycle problem worsens (AR and inventory don't shrink proportionally), leverage ratio rises, covenant breach risk escalates. PE recommendation: Company A is the clear acquisition candidate. (1) LBO potential: low current leverage means significant additional debt capacity ($750m+ at 5.5x Debt/EBITDA if EBITDA = $200m). (2) Working capital performance is already industry-leading — less operational risk. (3) Margin improvement may be possible at the margin (45% could become 48% with procurement optimization). Company B: avoid or heavy operational restructuring required. The 100-day CCC gap vs. A represents an enormous working capital improvement opportunity but also risk if the business deteriorates during the improvement program.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) CCC calculation for both, (2) identifying Company B's ROE as leverage-driven not operational, (3) DuPont decomposition linking to this, (4) Company A as LBO candidate with clear reasoning, (5) Company B risk identification, (6) structured memo format.

questions.topic: Capstone — Why Accounting Matters in PE/IB
questions.question: You are a first-year IB analyst. A managing director asks you: 'Why does a deal person need to understand financial accounting? Can't we just rely on the numbers the company gives us?' Write a one-page memo answering this question using concrete examples from what you have learned.
questions.model_answer: TO: Managing Director. RE: Why Deal Professionals Must Understand Financial Accounting. The short answer: accounting numbers are not objective facts — they are management's best (and sometimes most optimistic) interpretation of economic reality. A deal professional who relies on reported numbers without understanding their construction is systematically disadvantaged in negotiations, due diligence, and valuation. Three concrete areas where accounting literacy creates direct deal value: (1) Quality of Earnings directly affects deal price. EBITDA is the primary M&A valuation metric. But reported EBITDA can be inflated by: premature revenue recognition (inflated AR, rising DSO), LIFO liquidation (inventory declining, gross margin spike), and underprovision of AUA (thin allowance coverage). A QoE adjustment of $10m on a 10x EV/EBITDA deal reduces deal price by $100m. The analyst who identified this adjustment created $100m of value for the firm — more than most operational improvements. (2) Working capital affects the equity check dollar-for-dollar. NWC = AR + Inventory − AP. The NWC peg is negotiated. If DSO has been rising (AR building) and inventory days expanding, the seller is effectively leaving the buyer with a cash-absorbing business that requires immediate capital post-close. Understanding the CCC and its trajectory lets the deal team argue for a lower NWC target, reducing the equity check. (3) Post-acquisition goodwill and PPA determine the financial model. When we model post-acquisition earnings, we must account for: D&A step-up from asset revaluation, amortization of intangibles identified in PPA, and interest expense from deal debt. All three depress GAAP net income significantly. Without understanding these mechanics, the deal model is wrong — and management presentations to the IC will not hold up to scrutiny. Conclusion: accounting fluency is not a technical curiosity — it is the foundation of every valuation, every due diligence, and every deal model. The MD who can instantly read through the accounting to the economic reality underneath is better at every single step of deal execution.
questions.rubric: Award marks for: (1) directly addressing the question (accounting numbers are not objective), (2) QoE example with dollar impact, (3) NWC and equity check example, (4) PPA/post-acquisition model example, (5) persuasive, professional memo format.
